If any objective researcher reflects on the meaning of the words ‘no one can deliver it on your behalf except you or a man from yourself,’ they will note that he said, ‘no one can deliver it from for you (ʿanka) except you.’ He did not say, ‘no one can deliver it except you or a man from yourself’ as this would suggest that this person shared his status as a divine messenger. Nor did he say, ‘no one can deliver it on your behalf except a man from yourself,’ as this would include all of the other messages he charged the ordinary faithful to deliver on his behalf. The fact that he said: ‘no one can deliver it on your behalf except you or a man from yourself’ shows that he had duties as a divine messenger that only he could discharge and that no one else could undertake in his place except someone who was from himself and could be relied upon not to fail when acting in his stead. One of these duties was delivering new ordinances from God to the people.

I wonder, then, what led these scholars to ignore the revelation that God sent to the Prophet via Gabriel, that ‘no one can deliver it on your behalf except you or a man from yourself,’ and to explain it away as ‘the custom of the Arabs that a treaty could not be broken except by one of its parties or a man from his own household.’ After all, this custom of the Arabs is not recorded anywhere in the accounts of their history or battles, and this custom is not mentioned in any discussion except this one, concerning Sūrah Barāʾa, in which Ibn Kathīr mentions it and attributes it to other scholars.

Now, if it had indeed been the custom of the pre-Islamic Arabs to do this, what bearing does this custom have on Islam and what value does it have for the Prophet, given that barely a day went by without him abrogating a custom of the pre-Islamic era or breaking the traditions of his people? This custom does not reflect any lofty moral values or beneficial traditions, rather it embodies the tribal mentality of the pre-Islamic Arabs and the preferences of the clan elders. On the day he conquered Mecca, the Prophet is said to have stood before the Kaʿba and proclaimed: ‘Lo! Every exploit, every blood feud, and every claim to wealth is now beneath these two feet of mine, save for the custody of the House of God and quenching the thirst of the pilgrims!’ Even if this had been an inofiensive pre-Islamic custom, did the Prophet disregard it when he entrusted the verses to Abū Bakr and sent him to deliver them to the pilgrims in Mecca? Or did he forget it until, when Abū Bakr was already on his way, he suddenly remembered or was reminded by one of his companions? And even if this was the case, was he then obliged to observe this custom? The Prophet is the paragon of good character, and taking into account whatever needs taking into account is part of judiciousness and good sense. Therefore, how could those who reminded him neglect something so important in the first instance? A custom such as this is not something one simply forgets, any more than a warrior forgets his sword.

Was it a revelation from God that he should not disregard this noble Arab custom, and that it is now a divine ordinance, meaning that it is forbidden for the ruler of the Muslims to revoke a treaty unless he does it himself or entrusts it to a member of his household? What is the sense in such a ruling? Or was this a moral rule that the Prophet was obliged to observe because the idolaters would not have accepted the revocation of this treaty unless they heard it from him personally or from someone from his household? However, at this time, the Prophet was the one who had dominion over them, so who were they to decide whether or not they would accept such a revocation? He had the power to unilaterally revoke it, with or without their agreement. Or was it the case that the faithful were the ones being addressed by God’s words with whom you have made a treaty (9:1), an announcement from Allah and His M essenger (9:4), and kill the polytheists (9:5)? In which case, does this mean they would not have considered their treaty with the idolaters void unless they heard these words from the Prophet or a member of his household? Would they not have realized that the treaty was voided if they had simply heard the verses from Abū Bakr? If this were the case, then why would anyone who heard the announcement from Abū Hurayra, who proclaimed it until he lost his voice, accept that the treaty was voided? Was Abū Hurayra closer to ʿAlī than Abū Bakr was to the Prophet? The truth is that all of these narrations that portray Abū Hurayra and others proclaiming this message to the

people are inauthentic and should not be relied upon as historical accounts. In Tafsīr al-Manār, we read:

‘The collected narrations show that the Prophet sent Abū Bakr as the leader of the Hajj in the year 9 A.H. and commanded him to inform those idolaters who were performing the pilgrimage that they would not be allowed to perform it after this year. Then, he replaced Abū Bakr with ʿAlī so that the latter could inform them that their treaties were voided, that they had a grace period of four months to consider their options, that those treaties with fixed durations would be honored until their terms had expired, and to recite to them the verses

that contained these proclamations from the beginning of Sūrah Barāʾa. These are the first forty or thirty-three verses. The narrations appear to hesitate between these two numbers because some of them count in tens, counting a part thereof as a whole.

‘This is because the custom of the Arabs at the time was that treaties could only be broken by the one who made them or a member

of his close family. ʿAlī alone met this criterion, but the leadership of the Hajj remained with Abū Bakr, who helped ʿAlī carry out his duty and assigned some of the Companions such as Abū Hurayra to do this too.’

He also says:

‘Some of the Shīʿa blow ʿAlī’s appointment out of all proportion—as is their habit— and they add to it details from inauthentic sources that do not match what is known from reliable narrations. They claim that this demonstrates that ʿAlī was superior to Abū Bakr and, therefore, more entitled to succeed the Prophet than him. They claim that the Prophet relieved Abū Bakr of his duty to convey Sūrah Barāʾa because Gabriel commanded him to do this, and that he told him that no one could deliver it on his behalf except him or a man from himself. Furthermore, they do not confine this restriction to the breaking of treaties. In fact, they extend it to cover the entirety of the religion.

‘There is an abundance of authentic traditions to the effect that conveying the religion of Islam to others is a collective obligation upon

all the M uslims— in the same manner as defensive warfare (jihād)

is a collective obligation for the sake of protecting it— and that this is a duty, not a mark of superiority. One such tradition is what the Prophet said during the Farewell Pilgrimage (Hijjat al-Wadāʿ) to an audience of thousands: “Let those present convey this to those absent.” This statement is repeated in the two Ṣaḥīḥs of al-Bukhārī and Muslim and in other collections. In some accounts, Ibn ʿAbbās says: “For by He in whose hand is my soul, it was his last will and testament to his nation: ‘Let those present convey this to those absent.’”

Then there is the tradition: “Convey from me even but a single verse of the Qur’an.” Al-Bukhārī narrates it in his Ṣaḥīḥ and al-Tirmidhī narrates it in his Sunan. If it were not for sayings such as this, Islam would not have spread so quickly across the globe.

‘In fact, some of the Shīʿa reportedly claim that he removed Abū Bakr from his post as the leader of the Hajj and appointed ʿAlī in his place. This is a manifest falsehood that contradicts everything that has been narrated about this practical issue that is known to experts and laymen alike.

‘The truth is that ʿAlī—may God ennoble his countenance—was charged with conveying a specific message but, on that pilgrimage, he went as a follower of Abū Bakr, who had overall responsibility for overseeing the performance of this annual collective pillar of Islam. This was to the extent that it was Abū Bakr who told him when he should convey the message. Recall that he said: “Stand up, O ʿAlī and deliver the message of God’s Messenger.” Then he appointed some of the Companions to help him convey it to others, as we saw in the account of Abū Hurayra that is narrated in the two Ṣaḥīḥs and other works.’

The author (of Tafsīr al-Manār) then says that Abū Bakr’s leadership of the Hajj, combined with his leadership of the prayer in place of the Prophet during the latter’s final illness, constitutes clear evidence of his superiority above all of the other Companions and, therefore, his priority to succeed the Prophet.

As for his claim that there is an abundance of authentic traditions to the effect that conveying the religion of Islam to others is a collective obligation upon all the Muslims, this shows that he has not properly understood the meaning of the divine command that was revealed to the Prophet: ‘No one can deliver it on your behalf you except you or a man from yourself.’ He has failed to realize the difference between saying, ‘no one can deliver it on your behalf (ʿanka) except you or a man from yourself,’ and the saying, ‘no you can deliver it from you (minka) except you or a man from yourself.’ As a result of this confusion, he claims that if we take the former statement (‘on your behalf’) as categorical, this means that no one except the Prophet or a man from himself can convey any aspect of the religion to anyone else. Therefore, he believes that the abundant traditions commanding Muslims to convey their religion to others as a collective obligation refutes it and qualifies the statement, ‘no one can deliver it on your behalf…’, making it specific to conveying the revocation of the treaty and reducing God’s ordinance to a mere

pre-Islamic Arab custom.

This confusion of terms leads him to claim that reading the statement ‘no one can deliver it on your behalf’ as categorical would lead to people neglecting a duty that is considered essential by the totality of the M uslims, namely

the duty to convey the message of Islam to others. This is to the extent that he invokes evidence from the two Ṣaḥīḥs and other works in the form of the Prophetic saying: ‘Let those present convey this to those absent,’ and readers will already have noted that the Prophet’s statement, ‘no one can deliver it’ refers to new revelations, rather than the teachings of the religion as a whole. As for his claim, ‘In fact, some of the Shīʿa reportedly claim that he removed Abū Bakr from his post as the leader of the Hajj and appointed ʿAlī in his place. This is a manifest falsehood that contradicts everything that has been narrated about this practical issue that is known to experts and laymen alike,’ this is neither merely a claim or a falsehood (in fact, he is the one uttering falsehoods). On the contrary, this is an account reported in Shīʿī sources,

which we have presented above.

Disputes about the question of who led the Hajj pilgrimage that year are not our primary concern in discussing the statement, ‘No one can deliver it on your behalf you except you or a man from yourself.’ After all, whether Abū Bakr led the Hajj or whether ʿAlī did, and whether leading the Hajj indicated either of them were superior over the other, the fact is that leading the

pilgrimage falls within the scope of general Islamic authority, which is concerned with managing the daily affairs of M uslim society and implementing

the divine laws. It has nothing to do with divine knowledge or the contents of the revelation sent down from the heavens on matters of religious teaching. On the contrary, it is merely a function of the Prophet’s authority as a political leader to appoint Abū Bakr or ʿAlī as the leader of the Hajj. On another day, he gave Usāma ibn Zayd authority over Abū Bakr and all of the Companions on a military expedition. On another day, he appointed Ibn Umm Maktūm as the governor of Medina, even while the city had people superior to him living in it. He appointed someone else governor of Mecca after

its conquest, and another person still as governor of Yemen. He put someone else in charge of tax collection. He even made Abū Dajāna al-Sāʿidī or Sabbāʿ ibn ʿArfaṭa al-Ghafiārī (according to the Sīra of Ibn Hishām) governor of Medina in the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage before Abū Bakr had departed on the Hajj pilgrimage according to what has been narrated in al-Bukhārī, Muslim, Abū Dāwūd, al-Nasāʾī, and other collections. But none of this signifies anything more than the fact that these individuals were qualified for the

roles they were given— it certainly does not render them superior to all others. As for divine revelation, which contains God’s teachings and ordinances for mankind, the Prophet cannot delegate this task to someone who is lesser than him. Nor does anyone occupying positions of temporal authority over M uslim society have the right to deal with matters of revelation, whether by declaring verses general or particular, or confirming it or abrogating it. Furthermore, divine revelation is not dictated by the pre-Islamic customs of a particular people, such that it needs to accord with these in order to keep people happy.

By confusing these two distinct arenas of authority, we bring down the divine teachings from the apogee of dignity to the perigee of social thought, and reduce them to nothing more than norms, customs, and conventions. Thus, the human being explains metaphysical realities in a way that ordinary minds can comprehend and treats as important what society considers important rather than what God considers important, while neglecting what people

neglect, until it reaches the point that someone says that a divine revelation is nothing more than a pre-Islamic Arab custom.

If you ponder on the account of how the verses of repudiation were taken from Abū Bakr and given to ʿAlī as presented in these narrations, you find that the narrators have been surprisingly lax in their preservation of the material, even expanding them to include additional details from the narrators themselves (this is assuming that these accounts have not been distorted

to serve some agenda). For example, in the majority of them, we are told that the Prophet sent Abū Bakr to deliver the verses to the idolaters but then sent for ʿAlī and told him to take the verses from him and deliver them to the people instead, so Abū Bakr came back. In others, we are told that he sent Abū Bakr as the leader of the Hajj pilgrimage but then sent ʿAlī after him with the verses of Sūrah Barāʾa. Others still say that Abū Bakr himself told ʿAlī to convey the verses and then ordered other Companions to assist him in delivering the message.

M eanwhile, al-Ṭabarī and others relate from al-M ujāhid concerning the verse, A repudiation by Allah and His M essenger to the polytheists with whom you had made a treaty (9:1), that it concerned treaties between the M uslims and the Khuzāʿa, M udlij, and other tribes. According to this version of events, ‘God’s Messenger returned from the Battle of Tabūk and decided to perform the pilgrimage. However, when he arrived at the House of God, he saw the idolaters going about it in the nude and did not want to perform the pilgrimage so long as this was the case. So, he sent Abū Bakr and ʿAlī amongst the

people in Dhū al-Majāz and to the places where they were engaged in trade and throughout the pilgrimage season they went around and told those idolaters who had treaties with the Prophet that these treaties would expire no later than four months thence. These four months were the four consecutive sacred months—the twenty latter days of Dhū al-Hijja until the first ten of Rabīʿ alAwwal (sic), after which the treaty would be null and void and people would fight them until they were dead.’

If this is the case, then how can the author of Tafsīr al-Manār say that Shīʿī claims are ‘a manifest falsehood that contradicts everything that has been narrated about this practical issue that is known to experts and laymen alike’? If he means everyone at the time of the Prophet who saw this or heard about it first-hand from those who did, what benefit is this to us now?

If he meant that it was known to experts and laymen from the era immediately after that of the Prophet or the era that followed this, and that they knew

this and did not doubt it in the least, then why do there exist contradictory narrations from them that disagree on important details in their accounts? For example, some of them say that only ʿAlī could deliver the proclamation of repudiation, while others indicate that Abū Bakr helped him, and others still say that Abū Hurayra and other unnamed persons assisted with this. Some say that there were nine verses, while others say ten, and others still say sixteen, or thirty, or thirty-three, or thirty-seven, or forty, or the entirety of the chapter. Furthermore, accounts differ about what Abū Bakr did when ʿAlī took the verses from him. Some say that Abū Bakr continued on his way as the leader of Hajj, while others say that he came back, which has forced some commentators such as Ibn Kathīr to attempt to reconcile this by saying he only

returned after the pilgrimage was completed. But then, other accounts said that he came back to the Prophet to ask why he was relieved of his duty. In the narration of Anas that we shall consider below, the Prophet reportedly sent Abū Bakr with Sūrah Barāʾa, only to recall him and take the verses from him. Then there are reports that disagree on the day on which this announcement took place. Some say that the Hajj took place in the month of Dhū

al-Ḥijja and that the Greater Day of the Pilgrimage refers to all the days of the pilgrimage, or to the Day of ʿArafa, or to the Day of Slaughter, or to the day after the Day of Slaughter, or to other days entirely. Then there are accounts that say Abū Bakr performed the pilgrimage that year in Dhū al-Qaʿda. What about the four months grace period? Some reports say that this began in Shawwāl, others say it began in Dhū al-Qaʿda, while others say it began on the tenth of Dhū al-Ḥijja, and others still say it began on the eleventh of that month, and there are more reports and dates besides this. Some of these say the grace period corresponded to the pre-Islamic forbidden months of Dhū al-Qaʿda, Dhū al-Ḥijja, and M uḥarram, while others still say that it began on the day the message was delivered or on the day it was sent down by God. This is the state of disagreement between these narrations. W ith this in mind, how can anyone claim that anything about this was known to everyone, the experts and the laity alike? Bear in mind also that some of these explanations given above, even if they are statements from early commentators, the

statements of early commentators are no different in practice from traditions with incomplete chains of narration, and they should be treated as such. Now, let us address the claim in Tafsīr al-Manār that ‘the truth is that ʿAlī was charged with conveying a specific message but, on that pilgrimage, he went as a follower of Abū Bakr, who was the leader of the Hajj.’ There is no doubt that when the Prophet entrusted ʿAlī with delivering the verses of Barāʾa and the other four proclamations mentioned above, this was a special task. Recall, previously, that when Gabriel revealed to the Prophet, ‘No one can deliver it on your behalf except you or a man from yourself,’ he did not specify that this was in relation to the verses of repudiation. Therefore, we should not mix up the meaning of Gabriel’s statement with the specific mission given to ʿAlī on that journey.

As for the claim that ʿAlī was under Abū Bakr’s authority on that pilgrimage, this is something he has deduced from the account of Abū Hurayra.

However, we have already highlighted the problems with his retelling of events. (16) In al-Durr al-Manthūr, it is narrated from Ibn Abī Shayba, Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, and al-Tirmidhī and deemed reliable by Abū al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh from Anas: ‘The Prophet sent the repudiation with Abū Bakr, then he recalled him and said: “It does not behove anyone to convey this except a man from my own family (min ahlī),”

so he called ʿAlī and gave it to him.’

Author’s comments: Rashīd Riḍā—the author of Tafsīr al-Manār— argues that his statement, ‘or a man from myself,’ found in the narration of al-Sudayy, has been explained by other narrations in al-Ṭabarī and elsewhere, such as the phrase ‘or a man from my household (min ahl baytī).’ This, he says, refutes the claim that the phrase ‘from myself’ (minnī) means that the soul of ʿAlī is like the soul of God’s Messenger, or that he is akin to him, or that he is superior to all of the other Companions.

The narrations he is referring to are those which he previously cited: ‘And Aḥmad narrates with a reliable chain of narrators from Anas: “The Prophet sent the repudiation with Abū Bakr, but when he reached Dhū al-Ḥulayfa, he said: ‘None can convey this except a man from my own family (min ahlī),’ so he sent ʿAlī with them instead.”’ As you can see, this is almost identical to the narration from Anas we have already quoted above and—both contain the phrase ‘or a man from my own family’— and even where there are disparities in the wording, the meaning is essentially the same.

However, the problems with Rashīd Riḍā’s claims are as follows:

First, the phrase ‘or a man from myself’ (aw rajul minnī) only occurs in a single version of the tradition, with an incomplete (mawqūf) chain of narrators, namely the narration of al-Sudayy which he has already criticized as

weak (ḍaʿīf). Instead, the phrase ‘or a man from yourself’ (aw rajul minka) was used in the revelation from Gabriel that is recorded in the majority of the authentic narrations. Rashīd Riḍā further claims that the Prophet used the phrase ‘a man from my household’ (min ahl baytī) in many narrations when, in fact, there is only the single narration from Anas that uses this phrasing. Even then, it uses the word ahl (family) rather than ahl bayt (household). Second, these narrations— as has become clear— have been transmitted by meaning rather than by words. Therefore, you cannot use their vocabulary to explain the wording of Gabriel’s revelation that is recorded in the majority of authentic accounts of this event found in both Sunnī and Shīʿa collections of traditions.

Therefore, if the phrase min ahl baytī (from my household) was suitable to explain the phrases rajul minka (a man from yourself) or rajul minnī (a man from myself), then the same rule would apply to this narration and all of the other narrations with regard to the aforementioned narration from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī. In it, the Prophet says: ‘O ʿAlī, none can deliver this on my behalf except me or you.’ Therefore, can this not be adduced to explain the meaning of Anas’ narration ‘except a man from my household’ or ‘except a man from my family,’ and the other narrations as well, ‘except a man from yourself,’ and ‘except a man from myself.’ In which case, all of these phrases can be interpreted as references not only to the person of ʿAlī as being the only person suitable for the task at hand, but also to the idea that the soul of ʿAlī is like the soul (nafs) of the Prophet, as well as being from his family (ahl) and his household (ahl bayt). Therefore, by making this claim, Rashīd Riḍā ends up with precisely what he had hoped to avoid, and even more.

Third, the idea that ʿAlī is in the position of the Prophet’s self or soul (nafs) is not based solely on this one tradition and the phrase ‘rajul minnī,’ as Rashīd Riḍā seems to suppose. After all, if someone was to say: ‘so-and-so is from myself’ (fulān minnī), this would not imply that they considered this person to be like themselves in every aspect of their existence and a resemblance of them. On the contrary, such a statement would only indicate that there was some connection between them and that the other person shared some similarities with them. For example, look at Abraham’s statement: So whoever follows me is indeed from me (14:36). This is unless, of course, there is some contextual indication that the speaker intends a closer connection than this, for example, as we find in the verse: Any of you who allies with them is indeed one of them (5:51).

On the contrary, it is not understood merely from the phrase ‘a man from myself’ or ‘a man from yourself,’ but from the fact that this appears alongside the injunction: ‘No one can deliver it on your behalf except you.’ Now,

based on what we have already said, if Gabriel had said: ‘No one can deliver it on your behalf except you or a man from your family’ or ‘a man from your household,’ then we would deduce the same significance that we deduce from ‘No one can deliver it on your behalf except you or a man from yourself’ or ‘No one can deliver it on my behalf except me or a man from myself.’ This is in addition to the fact that he explains his decision to Abū Bakr using this phrase, when Abū Bakr could be seen as being ‘from himself’ by virtue of the fact that Abū Bakr was one of his followers.1 Fourth, Rashīd Riḍā neglects the abundant— or successively narrated (mutawātir)— authentic traditions that indicate that the Prophet’s Household are ʿAlī, Fāṭima, al-Ḥasan, and al-Ḥusayn, as we have already mentioned in our commentary on the Verse of Mubāhila and as we shall discuss in greater detail in our treatment of the Verse of Purification (Āyat al-Taṭhīr). At the time Sūrah Barāʾa was revealed, then, there was no man in the

1 In the narration of al-Ḥākim from Musʿab b. ʿAbd al-Raḥman, from his father, from the Prophet—quoted below—he tells the people of Ṭāʾif: ‘By He in whose hand is my soul, you will surely establish the prayer and pay the zakāt, or I will send against you a man from myself’ or ‘a man like myself.’ People thought that when he said this, he meant Abū Bakr or ʿUmar, but then he took the hand of ʿAlī and said: ‘I will send this one,’ to remove any doubts about whom he had meant. Prophet’s Household except ʿAlī, which would mean that no matter which of these phrases was used (‘a man from myself,’ ‘a man from my family,’ or ‘a man from my household’), it was intended as an allusion to Imām ʿAlī. This leaves us with the same conclusion as above.

Rashīd Riḍā seems to believe that the phrase ‘from my household’ (min ahl baytī) is of broad scope, encompassing all of the Prophet’s relatives from the Banū Hāshim or from the Banū Hāshim and his womenfolk. In interpreting it in this manner, he renders it an ordinary term and removes any

special distinction from being conferred upon the members of the Prophet’s Household. With this in mind, the meaning of the statement becomes ‘no one can annul the treaty on my behalf except a man from the Banū Hāshim.’ However, this reading depends upon us looking only at the meaning of these words in everyday language, rather than considering their significance within the framework of the religion. We have already discussed this in relation to the words ibn (son) and bint (daughter) when debating whether the son of a man’s daughter can also be called his son by extension. There are those who base their argument purely on the conventions of language, namely whether or not the standard usage of the language allows such a claim. However, this represents a confusion between the two realms of vocabulary and meaning, or between social conventions and divine religious ones, as we have already explained elsewhere.

However, possibly the strangest claim that Rashīd Riḍā makes is that the tradition he cites is an explicit and unambiguous (naṣṣ) refutation of the Shīʿī understanding of the phrase ‘from myself’ (minnī). In other words, he believes that the phrase ‘from my household’ (min ahl baytī) explicitly and unambiguously shows that the meaning of ‘from myself’ means ‘from the Banū Hāshim.’

However, we have no idea from whence he produces the claim that the phrase ahl al-bayt explicitly and unambiguously denotes the Banū Hāshim. After all, there are countless narrations to the effect that the ahl al-bayt of the Prophet are ʿAlī and Fāṭima and their two sons al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn. How then, can he assert that ‘my household’ (ahl baytī) refers to the Banū Hāshim as a whole and then, from that, claim that ‘from myself’ also refers to the Banū Hāshim as a whole? This is an utterly untenable thesis.

(17) In Tafsīr al-ʿAyyāshī, it is narrated from Zurāra, Ḥumrān, and Muḥammad ibn Muslim from Imām al-Bāqir and Imām al-Ṣādiq about the verse Travel in the land for four months (9:2): ‘The last twenty days of Dhū al-Ḥijja, the months of Muḥarram, Ṣafar, and Rabīʿ al-Awwal, then the first ten days of Rabīʿ al-Ākhar.’

Author’s comments: There are countless narrations in Shīʿī collections from the Imāms of the Prophet’s Household to the effect that this is what the phrase four months in the aforementioned verse. This is narrated by al-Kulaynī, al-Ṣadūq, al-ʿAyyāshī, al-Qummī, and others in their works. It has also been narrated in Sunnī collections. However, Sunnīs narrate other traditions that contradict this interpretation, including some which claim that Abū Bakr performed the pilgrimage with the people in the year 9 A.H. during the month of

Dhū al-Qaʿda. However, these are unsubstantiated, so we have omitted them. (18) In Tafsīr al-ʿAyyāshī, it is narrated from Ḥakīm ibn Jubayr, from ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn, concerning the verse, And an announcement from Allah and His Messenger (9:3): ‘An announcement by the Commander of the Faithful.’

Author’s comments: This meaning has also been narrated by Ḥurayz from Imām al-Ṣādiq, and by Jābir from both him and Imām al-Bāqir.

Al-Qummī narrates a tradition from his father, from Faḍḍāla, from Abān ibn ʿUthmān, from Ḥakīm ibn Jubayr, from ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn, in which he relates the following words of Imām ʿAlī: ‘I was the one who delivered the announcement to the people.’ Al-Ṣadūq transmits the same via a chain of narrators going back to Ḥakīm from him. It is narrated in al-Durr al-Manthūr

from Ibn Abī Ḥātim, from Ḥaīm ibn Ḥamīd, from ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn. In Tafsīr al-Burhān, we read: ‘Al-Sudayy and Abū Mālik and Ibn ʿAbbās and Zayn al-ʿĀbidīn say: “The announcement was delivered by ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib.”’ (19) Also in Tafsīr al-Burhān, it is narrated via al-Ṣadūq, via his chain of narrators from al-Fuḍayl ibn ʿAyyāḍ, from Imām al-Ṣādiq. Al-Fuḍayl asked him asked about the Day of the Greater Pilgrimage (9:3). He responded: ‘Do you know anything about it?’ The narrator replied:

‘Yes, Ibn ʿAbbās used to say: The Day of the Greater Pilgrimage is the Day of ʿArafa until sunrise on the Day of Slaughter, meaning that whoever participated in the Day of ʿArafa had participated in the Hajj, but that whoever missed it had missed the Hajj. Therefore, it goes from the eve of ʿArafa until the end of the night that follows it. The evidence for that is that whoever reaches the eve of the Day of Slaughter before sunrise is said to have reached Hajj on time.

Therefore, the eve of the Day of Slaughter is considered part of the Day of ʿArafa.’

Then Imām al-Ṣādiq said: ‘The Commander of the Faithful said, “The Day of the Greater Pilgrimage is the Day of Slaughter.” And he supported this with God’s saying: Travel in the land for four months, which is the last twenty days of Dhū al-Ḥijja, the months of M uḥarram, Ṣafar, and Rabīʿ al-Awwal, then the first ten days of Rabīʿ al-Ākhar. If The Day of the Greater Pilgrimage was the Day of ʿArafa, then the idolaters would have been given four months and a day to travel in the land. He further supported this with the passage, and an announcement from Allah and His Messenger to the people on the Day of the Greater Pilgrimage, saying: “I was the one who delivered the announcement to the people.”’

Al-Fuḍayl asked: ‘Then what is the meaning of this phrase, the Greater Pilgrimage (al-Ḥajj al-Akbar)?’ He replied: ‘It is only called “greater” because it took place in the only year in which both the Muslims and the idolaters made the pilgrimage. The idolaters did not perform the Hajj in following years.’

(20) In the same source it is narrated from him, via his chain of narrators leading to Muʿāwiya ibn ʿAmmār, who related: ‘I asked Abū

ʿAbdallāh about the Day of the Greater Pilgrimage. He said: “The Day of Slaughter and the lesser ʿumra.”’

Author’s comments: In addition to associating the Day of the Greater Pilgrimage with the Day of Slaughter, the above narration also explains why it was called the Day of the “Greater” Pilgrimage. All of the narrations of the Imāms of the Prophet’s Household, barring those which are irregular (shādhdh), say that the Day of the Greater Pilgrimage mentioned in the verse was a reference to the Day of Slaughter, which fell on the tenth of Dhū al-Ḥijja. They narrate this from Imām ʿAlī.

Al-Kulaynī narrates this tradition in al-Kāfī from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Muʿāwiya ibn ʿAmmār, from Imām al-Ṣādiq. He also narrates it via Dhurayḥ from him, as does Shaykh al-Ṣadūq. Al-ʿAyyāshī narrates it from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, Ibn Udhayna, and al-Fuḍayl ibn ʿAyyāḍ, from him as well.

(21) In al-Durr al-M anthūr, it is narrated from Ibn Mardawayh, from Ibn Abī Awfā, from the Prophet, that he said on ʿĪd al-Aḍḥā: ‘This is the Day of the Greater Pilgrimage.’

(22) In the same source, al-Bukhārī, Abū Dāwūd, Ibn Māja, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Abū Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, and Abū Muʿaym in al-Ḥilya narrate from Ibn ʿUmar that the Messenger of God stood on the Day of Slaughter between the stone pillars (jamārāt) while he performed his Hajj pilgrimage and asked of those assembled: ‘What is today?’ They responded: ‘It is the Day of Slaughter.’ He said: ‘Today is the Day of the Greater Pilgrimage.’ Author’s comments: This has been narrated via various routes from ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās, Mughīra ibn Shuʿba, Abū Juḥayfa, and ʿAbdallāh ibn Abī Awfā. It has also been narrated by various routes from the Prophet that it is the Day of ʿArafa. This has also been narrated from ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn alZubayr. M eanwhile, it is narrated from Saʿīd ibn al-M usayyab that it the day after the Day of Slaughter. It has also been narrated that it is all the days of the

pilgrimage, and that it is the pilgrimage in the year that Abū Bakr performed the Hajj. The latter most of these reports is compatible with the tradition reported from Imām al-Ṣādiq, above, in which he said that it was called the Day of the Greater Pilgrimage because it was the year in which the idolaters and the Muslims both made the pilgrimage.

(23) In Tafsīr al-ʿAyyāshī, it is narrated from Zurāra, from Imām al-Bāqir, concerning the verse, Then, when the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists wherever you find them, capture them and besiege them

(9:5): ‘(The period of grace) lasted from the Day of Slaughter to the tenth of Rabīʿ al-Ākhar.

authentic a tradition from Muʿab ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from his father: ‘The Messenger of God conquered Mecca, then he went to Ṭāʾif and besieged it for seven or eight consecutive days, then he besieged it alternatively. but then he took the hand of ʿAlī and said: “I will send this one.”’

(25) In Tafsīr al-ʿAyyāshī, a tradition narrated by Jābir from Imām al-Bāqir reads: ‘Yet if they repent means: “If they believe, then they are your brethren in faith.”’

Author’s comments: A similar account is also narrated by al-ʿAyyāshī in his Tafsīr from Abū ʿUthmān the Muezzin, Abū al-Ṭufayl, and al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī. Shaykh al-Ṭūsī also narrates this from Abū ʿUthmān the M uezzin in his Amālī. In his tradition, Bakīr says: ‘I asked Abū Jaʿfar (al-Bāqir) about this. He said: “The shaykh has spoken truthfully. This is what ʿAlī said. This is how it was.”’
