‘In the peace treaty signed between the Messenger of God and the Quraysh on the Day of Ḥudaybiyya, it was stipulated that whoever wished to make a treaty or alliance with the Prophet was free to do so, and whoever wanted to make a treaty or alliance with the Quraysh was free to do so. The Khuzāʿa hastened forth and said: “We will make an alliance with Muḥammad.” Then the Banū Bakr hastened forth and said: “We will make an alliance with the Quraysh.” And this peace endured for about seventeen or eighteen months.

‘Then, the Banū Bakr, who were allies of the Quraysh, launched an attack by night on the Khuzāʿa, who were allies of God’s Messenger, at a well that belonged to them in the vicinity of Mecca known as al-Watīr. The Quraysh imagined that God’s Messenger would not know what had happened under the cover of dark, so they supplied the Bakr with weapons and mounts and, because of the hatred they had towards the Prophet, they even participated directly in the attack on al-Watīr.

‘ʿAmr ibn Sālim rode to Medina with news of what had happened at al-Watīr and addressed the Messenger of God with the following verses of poetry:

“O Lord, I implore Muḥammad / by the oath of our father and his of old,

You were are sons for whom we provided the mother / then we submitted and never withdrew our hand,

So help us, God guide you / and call God’s servants to our aid, Among them the Messenger of God, sword-drawn / when he is wronged his face becomes overcast with anger, In a great army heaving like the sea / surely the Quraysh have broken their promise to you,

And they have violated their solemn oath to you / and they tried to prevent me from warning you,

They claim that I will find no one to help us / and they are but a miserable few,

They attacked us by night in al-Watīr / and killed us as we bowed and prostrated.”

‘So the Messenger of God said: “We will come to your aid, O ʿAmr ibn Sālim.” Then, a cloud appeared in the sky and he said: “This cloud shall witness (our) assistance to the Banū Kaʿb.” Then he ordered the people to muster for war (jihād) and to keep their departure a secret. He invoked God and asked Him to blind the Quraysh to his movements so that they might catch them by surprise in their homeland.’

Author’s comments: This narration is reported in al-Durr al-Manthūr, along with accounts from Mujāhid and ʿIkrima about the Quraysh’s violation of the treaty of Ḥudaybiyya and their support for the Banū Bakr against the Messenger of God’s allies the Khuzāʿa. They say that this was the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzūl) for the verses W ill you not make war on a people who broke their pledges… and heal the hearts of a faithful folk (9:13–14). The ‘faithful folk’ in this instance are the Khuzāʿa.

If this is indeed accurate, then this would mean that the verse W ill you not make war on a people who broke their pledges… and the three subsequent verses (9:13–16) were, in fact, revealed prior to the conquest of M ecca and, therefore, before the verses of repudiation.

However, regarding the account narrated by Ibn Isḥāq and al-Bayhaqī, even if we treat it as authentic because it is narrated by al-Masrūr ibn M akhrama, al-M asrūr’s narration does not explicitly state that the verses in question were revealed in response to this event. Neither can we rely on the account from Mujāhid and ʿIkrima both because it has an incomplete chain of narrators and because the context of these verses does not lend credence to the idea that they were revealed before the conquest of M ecca. These verses are clearly connected to the verses from the beginning of the chapter and thus were revealed at the same time.

As for the verse, who broke their pledges and resolved to expel the M essenger, and opened against you initially, even if the description it contains is especially apt for the Quraysh, it could equally apply to the Quraysh’s allies and neighbors who had not yet converted following the conquest of Mecca. Therefore,

because of their solidarity with the Quraysh and relationship with them, the verse ascribes to them the same attributes as the Quraysh originally had. Know also that there are various narrations in Shīʿī sources from the Prophet’s Household that apply these verses to the circumstances surrounding the advent of Imām al-Mahdi. However, this is an example of extending

the meaning of the verses to a new context (al-jarī).

On the Meaning of ‘Treaty’ (ʿahd), its Types, and Some of its Rules

At the beginning of the sixth volume of this work, we touched on the meaning of the terms ʿaqd (agreement) and ʿahd (treaty). Hence, we will begin by recapitulating what was previously stated, before discussing the various types of treaty and the rules pertaining to them in a new format divided into a number of sections.

First: On the origins of contracts in general From the many discussions we have presented in this work so far, it should be clear to the reader that, over the course of his life, the human being always conceives of his actions and the material things that they are related to as actually existing objective realities and represents them as such. As such, he applies the same rules to them as he applies to objective reality, such as the universal laws that govern the cosmos, in a manner that accords with his aims in life. For example, he might take a series of distinct units of sound, such as z, y, and d, and combine them in a specific form to produce the word zayd. He then posits that zayd refers to a human being who exists in objective reality and names him ‘Zayd.’ Then, whenever he wants to evoke the thought of this person in the mind of a listener, he utters the word ‘Zayd’ to him. Therefore, this word becomes a representation of the real being Zayd for him and, in doing this, he achieves his goal.

And when a person wishes to bring about some action that can only be performed by a group of people working together, then he will assemble a group and conceive of them as one body. Then, he will choose one of them to perform the role in relation to the rest of the group as the head does for the rest of the body, and he calls this person ‘the head’ of the group. At the same he conceives of the remainder of the group’s members as the limbs of this body, referring to them as ‘members’ (member is an archaic term for ‘limb’ in English, just as the Arabic term ʿaḍuww can signify both the member of a group and a limb of a body). Then, he applies the same rules to the head of the group in the same way as he would to the head of a body, and likewise the same rules to the members of the group as he would to the limbs of a body. With proper analysis, it is evident that all human ideas about society devolve to this, whether directly or through the mediation of other concepts and arguments. The same is true of the human being’s personal thoughts with regard to his behavior and actions.

The human being treats making contracts, fulfilling agreements, and everything that pertains to oaths, vows, and pledges with the utmost seriousness. The primary reason for this is that the human being’s overriding priority

is to preserve his life, attain his goals, and secure the happiness that flows from his life taking its proper course.

So, whenever the human being attains something that he desires and gains power over it, he begins to enjoy it however is most appropriate, such as eating, drinking, and other such things, with the faculties of enjoyment with which he has been endowed. Likewise, he removes any obstacles to this enjoyment that he encounters on his way and believes that he is only able to accomplish this because of the power he has been granted.

One of the tools with which the human being has been furnished is his intellectual capital, through which he is able to plan his life, improve his livelihood, complete his work today, and make preparations for his work tomorrow. His actions, which are either directly concerned with acting upon matter

or ultimately devolve to this, are entirely dependent upon the extent of his power to act and his possession of everything that he needs in order to act. However, these actions also differ from one another in that some of them can be accomplished with little effort and in minimal time. For example, a hungry person comes upon some food and eats it. This does not require any power greater than the amount of time it takes to perform the act, nor does such an act require any preparations to be made or preliminary steps to be followed. By contrast, the overwhelming majority of human social activities require considerable power to be expended in order to be realized, both at the time of their performance, as well as both before and, in some cases, even afterwards. This is because these acts have preliminary steps that must be traversed and preparations that must be made in advance of their coming to be. Very little of what the human being does in life is by accident. On the contrary, most matters of human existence require the ground to be prepared in order for them to come into being at the desired time.

One aspect of this preparation is to obtain and organise all of the necessary means for an action, and another is to remove any obstacles that might

stand in its way. In short, the human being will not succeed in an action or see the results of his efforts unless he has ensured that all of the necessary ingredients for success are present and all of the barriers and impediments to it have been removed.

It is the realization of this truth that leads the human being to turn to his compatriots in order to ensure his own success, whether by seeking assistance from them to obtain the necessary ingredients for his success or ensuring that they will not act to thwart his efforts or prevent him from removing the barriers that stand before him.

For example, if a person is in need of clothes— even relatively simple garments made from a plain material such as cotton or wool—attaining this goal

depends on numerous intermediary steps: Someone must spin the cotton or wool into thread, which someone must then weave into fabric, which someone must then tailor into clothes. And the spinner, the weaver, and the tailor

all depend on someone to manufacture the tools they use in their respective trades. Without all of these steps being fulfilled, this person will not manage to find a set of clothes. Therefore, he needs his compatriots to help him in achieving his goal by wedding their efforts to his and not leaving him to his own devices, or else he will never succeed.

Equally, someone who wishes to settle on some land or take up residence in some house will not be able to reach his new home or live in it unless people allow him to pass and do not prevent him from doing with his home as he sees fit.

It is these needs and requirements that lead the human being to recognise the importance of making agreements and signing contracts with others, as this allows him to join his actions to the actions of others in the same way as one connects two pieces of rope with one knot. These agreements also require him to act reciprocally by helping others achieve their goals through fulfilling his side of the agreement and not interfering with their activities.

This is the foundation upon which all the contracts and agreements concluded between people rest, including marriage, commerce, and the like thereof. These are both contracts and an example of covenants in a general sense, because the general meaning of a covenant is that a person should give a promise or a written contract to the effect that they will perform a certain beneficial action for the other party or that they will not hinder them from undertaking a certain action, whether for a specified period of time or indefinitely.

This general meaning of covenant or agreement is the focus of our present discussion and not specific forms of agreements with special names such as contracts of sale, marriage contracts, or other transactions, because this kind of agreement is not relevant to the subject we wish to address here. This is because each of them have their own specific rules and legal effects in different human societies. Instead, we want to discuss the general concept of a covenant, in the sense of an agreement one human makes with another to help or not to hinder them in various social goals, and the implications of this for human existence. For example, if one person agrees to pay another a specified sum of money annually in order to help him obtain certain needs or in exchange for certain benefits. Alternatively, he might agree not to interfere with his work or prevent him from attaining a specified goal for a certain period of time, or indefinitely. These sorts of agreements are not broken unless one of the two parties breaks them or unless both parties agree to set them aside.

Perhaps, in addition to signing an agreement, a person might also swear an oath. This means that the party in question links this agreement to something he considers sacred and inviolable, as if he is assigning the same sanctity and inviolability to the agreement itself. In this way, he provides a guarantee that he will fulfil his responsibilities as stipulated by the agreement, or else he robs the object of his oath of its sanctity and respect. One might say: ‘By God, I will not betray you,’ or ‘by my life, I will support you,’ or ‘I swear that I will come to your aid.’ In uttering such an oath, the person agrees that if they break their oath, it is as though they have voided the sanctity of their Lord, the sanctity of their life, or the sanctity of their honor.

Or perhaps a covenant or agreement might be sealed through a pledge, whereby one party places his hand in the hand of another, symbolizing that he has given him the hand with which he will perform the act. In other words, he will not do anything that the other party dislikes, because he has placed his hand in theirs.

Second: The need of societies for contracts and agreements These agreements and covenants are needed by both human beings and human societies alike, as a society is nothing more than a collection of individuals. Therefore, the life of a society is the sum of the lives of its members,

and the actions of a society are the sum of the activities of its members. Equally, good and evil, benefit and harm, health and disease, progress and growth, uprightness and deviance, happiness and misery, and, ultimately, survival and collapse, all depend on the sum of these individuals.

Therefore, society is a macro-person, with similar needs and goals as the individuals that constitute its body politic. This means that the relationship between one society and another is akin to the relationship between one person and another. In securing these goals and engaging in activities, a society

has similar needs to the human being in terms of security and safety. In fact, a society’s needs for these things are even more acute than that of an individual, because the greater the agent, the greater the goal, and the greater the action needed to obtain it. Therefore, a society requires safety and security from its members lest it disintegrate or collapse, and it needs safety and security from other rival societies.

As the history of past nations and peoples has shown, and as we can ourselves observe from the condition of the nations of our own time, it is the

nature of all human societies to form agreements with other societies in order to meet their political, economic, cultural and other needs. This is because no society can grow or develop except through cooperation with others like it and the absence of opposition from them.

Third: The validity of treaties in Islam and the obligation to respect them

Islam aims to reform the social life of human beings just as it aims to reform their individual lives. Therefore, it provides general laws addressing the collective life of human beings, such as the laws of jihād, defence, and fighting against aggressors and treaty breakers, as well as laws about peace, treaties, and agreements.

The kind of treaty that we are discussing at present is one that Islam has endorsed fully and without qualification. As such, violating it without justification is considered one of the gravest sins imaginable, unless of course one

side has already violated it and the other is merely responding in kind. In the Qur’an, God orders people to uphold their agreements and contracts and condemns those who violate them in the strongest possible terms. He says: O you who have faith! Keep your agreements (5:1); But as for those who break Allah’s compact after having pledged it solemnly…it is such on whom the curse will lie, and for them will be the ills of the (ultimate) abode (13:25); and fulfil the covenants; indeed all covenants are accountable (17:34), and more besides. God has not permitted the breaking of treaties or agreements except where there is a valid justification. For example, if one side violates a treaty through aggression or wrongdoing, or if it is likely to be violated because they have put it aside, then there is no problem with likewise disregarding the treaty, nor is this blameworthy. God says: And if you fear treachery from a people, break off with them in a like manner. Indeed Allah does not like the treacherous (8:58). Therefore, God permits the breaking of a treaty when one fears the treachery of the other side. However, He requires that the Muslims inform the other side of the treaty’s termination and does not permit them to launch a surprise attack: break offwith them in a like manner. It is obligatory to inform them that the treaty has been revoked to avoid being accused of perfidious behavior. He says: A repudiation by Allah and His M essenger to the polytheists with whom you had made a treaty: Travel in the land for four months (9:1–2). Notice also that God does not simply repudiate the treaty but gives them a period of grace in which to consider their situation and decide on what course of action they would like to take. If they wish, they can believe and be saved, or if they do not, they can be fought and destroyed. One of the positive effects of giving the Arab idolaters a deadline was that they chose to believe rather than fight. And God completes this grace towards them by issuing the following ordinance after the repudiation: If any of the polytheists seeks asylum from you, grant him asylum until he hears the Word of Allah. Then convey him to his place of safety. That is because they are a people who do not know (9:6).

He also exempts those who have adhered faithfully to their treaties: How shall the polytheists have any treaty with Allah and His M essenger?! (Barring those with whom you made a treaty at the Holy Mosque; so long as they are steadfast with you, be steadfast with them. Indeed Allah loves the Godwary). How? For if they get the better of you, they will observe toward you neither kinship nor covenant. They please you with their mouths while their hearts spurn

you; and most of them are transgressors (9:7–8). Notice that God explains why the M uslims should be steadfast with those idolaters who are steadfast with them— because this is part of Godwariness (taqwā), which is the very essence of that to which the religion of Islam is calling mankind, for God loves those who are Godwary. This rationale for upholding treaties is not bound to a particular context but remains valid until the Day of Judgement.

God also says: So should anyone aggress against you, assail him in the manner he assailed you (2:194), and Ill feeling for a people should not lead you, because they barred you from (entering) the Holy M osque, to transgress. Cooperate in piety and Godwariness, but do not cooperate in sin and aggression, and be wary of Allah (5:2).

As for being the first to violate a treaty without the other side providing any justification for this, this is forbidden in the upright religion. We have already encountered the verses of the Qur’an: so long as they are steadfast with you, be steadfast with them and but do not transgress. Indeed Allah does not like transgressors (2:190).

These were the principles that guided the actions of the Prophet throughout his life. He made a treaty with the Banū Qaynuqāʿ, the Banū Qurayẓa,

and other Jewish tribes, and he did not violate the protocols of those treaties except after the other side did so first. He made a treaty with the Quraysh at Ḥudaybiyya and he did not break this treaty until they broke it by supporting the Banū Bakr against the Khuzāʿa, who were allies of the Prophet, while the Banū Bakr were allies of the Quraysh.

As for violating the terms of a treaty without the other side violating them first, there is no justification for this in Islam, even if adhering to the treaty is prejudicial to the interests of the Muslims or exposes them to some harm, even if they are able to defend their interests with force or can find some excuse to circumvent their agreements in such a way that they will not be subject to blame or reproach. However, Islam has not allowed them to act in such a way, for the criterion here is not their material interests but the truth, and the truth has only ever harmed those that strayed from it and sought something other than it.

Fourth: Comparing Islam to non-religious societies in terms of respect for treaties and agreements

Human societies, especially ones which are highly developed— albeit nonreligious—have no higher aim or purpose for coming together or following

their established traditions except to enjoy the benefits of material life to the greatest degree possible. As a result, they do not need to do anything other than uphold the practical laws that facilitate their various pursuits in life. Therefore, it is clear that, in such an environment, there is no value for spiritual matters save for the extent to which they relate to and support the aims of material existence. Spiritual virtues such as honesty, chivalry, compassion, and the like thereof have no value unless they bring tangible benefits to

society and so long as they do not cause any inconvenience to those in power if they do not. Therefore, there is no impetus to uphold them. In fact, the impetus is to discard them.

This is why official bodies and governing of  cials in such societies do not believe that they have any duty or function other than to safeguard the society’s material interests. Hence, they only enter into treaties and agreements

based on their current interests. They measure their own strength and needs, measure those of the other side, consider any other relevant factors, and draw up an agreement based on these calculations.

So long as these power calculations remain unchanged, the treaty will remain unchanged. However, if one side or the other gains the upper hand over the other, they will invalidate the treaty on the basis of some pretext or allegations manufactured and contrived for that purpose. Indeed, they only offer

these as excuses in order to maintain the façade of adhering to international laws, and they do not see any consequences to breaking these laws worthy of consideration except those that threaten their own material interests or those of the society that they govern. Were this not the case, they would violate their agreements at the slightest excuse.

Such societies are not prevented by morality or spirituality from lying, treachery, or infringing on the other party’s rights, as none of these things hold any value to them; they only consider how to safeguard the material interests of their own society and how best to achieve its goals. And if the reader pays close attention to conflicts that occurred between different societies, both recently and in history, especially to the conflicts that are taking place in the current era, they will note that there are many treaties and agreements that have been broken in the way we have just described.

By contrast, Islam does not consider the material life of the human being to be their real life, nor does it consider the enjoyment of material benefits to be true happiness. On the contrary, it sees real life as residing in the union of matter with spirit and finds the attainment of true happiness in securing felicity in both this world and the next. Therefore, it must promulgate laws for regulating life in accordance with the human being’s God-given nature (fiṭra) and not only based on what the human being sees as profitable for himself. And it must issue a call to follow the truth and be guided by it rather than following one’s own desires and obeying the whims of the majority that are founded on their own emotions and prejudices. God says: So set your heart on the religion as a people of pure faith, the origination of Allah according to which He originated mankind. There is no altering Allah’s creation; that is the upright religion (30:30); It is He who has sent His Apostle with the guidance and the religion of truth, that He may make it prevail over all religions, though the polytheists should be averse (9:33); Rather W e have brought them the truth

(23:90); Had the Truth followed their desires, the heavens and the earth would have surely fallen apart (along) with those who are in them (23:71).

In order for a virtuous society to exist, it is necessary that it adopts true beliefs, virtuous morals, and good deeds together. M atter cannot suffice without spirit, but neither can spirit survive without matter. Therefore, such a society must adhere to human virtues, whether these are materially beneficial or

not, and avoid vices, whether these are materially harmful or not, because that is what it means to follow the truth. And none will truly come to harm except those who stray from the middle path or overstep the bounds of the truth. Based on this, we can understand why God repudiates the treaty of the idolaters, because they have already repudiated it through their actions. However, His mercy also leads him to grant them four months grace and to enjoin the Muslims to uphold the treaties of those idolaters who upheld theirs, for events have weakened them to the point that they are humbled before the might of Islam. Equally, God commands His Prophet, should he fear the treachery of a people, to repudiate his treaty with them, so long as he informs them of this fact, as God does not like treachery or deceit.

On Attributing Actions to Higher Causes

About the verse, Make war on them so that Allah may punish them by your hands (9:14), we have already discussed on several occasions in this commentary how philosophical arguments show that just as phenomena can be attributed to their immediate causes (asbāb qarība), they can also be attributed to their ultimate causes (asbāb qaṣwā), which are the causes of their immediate causes. Therefore, these phenomena can be simultaneously described as the effects of these ultimate causes and as the effects of their immediate causes. For example, movement depends upon the action of a mover, and the movement of this mover depends upon its mover. This is like a series of cogs, where the first cog is moved by the second, which is moved by the third in turn.

Therefore, an action is related to the agent that caused it, but it is also related to its agent’s cause, and this second relationship is not distinct or independent from the first. This means that the immediate cause’s relationship to the higher cause is like that of a tool. In other words, it plays a purely

intermediary role in bringing about the effect, in the sense that it does not act independently of its own cause, and if its cause did not exist, neither it nor its effect would exist either.

However, this does not mean that the intermediary agent is unaware of what it does, or that it does not do it of its own free will and volition. On the contrary, it is a conscious agent (fāʿil shāʿir), but it did not endow itself with this consciousness. Rather, its own cause is what gave it this consciousness, as it created both the intermediary agent and its consciousness. The same is true of its free-will, but the free-willed agent did not endow itself with this. Rather, the cause that brought it into being also gave it free-will. And just as an effect depends upon a cause, even when there is neither consciousness nor freewill, it depends upon the cause of its cause in exactly the same way. Equally,

a conscious or free-willed action depends upon its cause (the conscious and free-willed agent), and it depends upon the cause of its cause (which brought into being the conscious and free-willed agent) in exactly the same way. In other words, the cause of the conscious or free-willed agent wanted the conscious or free-willed agent to produce the desired effect through its conscious action or of its own volition. Therefore, the higher cause not only desired the intermediary to perform the action, it also desired the intermediary to perform the action consciously and of its own free will. It is not the case that it merely wanted the intermediary to perform the action, whether it was of its own volition or not.

It is based on this reality that human beings proceed, according to their intuitive understanding, to attribute a phenomenon to its ultimate cause in the same way they attribute it to its immediate cause, in that it is an effect that emanates from it. One might say: ‘So-and-so built a house and dug a well,’ when it was the builder who built the house and the well-digger who dug the well. Equally, one might say: ‘The king had so-and-so lashed, and so-and-so executed, and so-and-so imprisoned, and went to war with such-and-such a people,’ when it was the scourger who delivered the whipping, the executioner who put someone to death, the gaoler who imprisoned someone, and the soldiers who went to war. One might also say: ‘X burned the clothes of Y,’ even

though the clothes were burned by fire, or ‘X cured Y of his illness,’ when it was the medicine he took that cured him and X only prescribed it to him. In all of these cases, it is the order or request of the ultimate cause that is said to

have brought about the action of the immediate cause, hence the action of the immediate cause is attributed to the ultimate cause. However, even though the ultimate cause did not directly perform the action, the attribution of it to him is nevertheless genuine (ḥaqīqa) and not merely figurative (majāz). Some grammarians and others argue that all of this falls within the scope of figurative speech because it is possible to negate the action from the ultimate cause. They say that the owner of the house did not lay a single brick in its construction, rather it was the builder who did this. However, they are only looking at action insofar as it emanated from its immediate cause, when it is self-evident that such direct action (mubāshara) is the function of the immediate cause, and we do not dispute this. Instead, what we are arguing is that we

can conceive of this action as depending upon a higher cause as well. That is why we say that just as the immediate cause performs the act, the higher cause acts upon the immediate cause and, in doing so, causes him to perform that act. It is this point that forces them to distinguish between different kinds of actions and attribute some of these to both the immediate and ultimate cause jointly, while assigning others to only the immediate cause who undertakes the act itself. Therefore, they say that those acts whose very concept implies direct involvement with their performance can only be ascribed to the immediate cause. For example, eating in the sense of chewing and swallowing, drinking in the sense of sipping and swallowing, or sitting down. Hence, when a master orders his servant to eat food, or drink water, or sit on a chair, one cannot

say that the master ate, drank, or sat, rather one must say that the servant ate, drank, and sat. On the other hand, one can say that the master disposed of some property or gave money to someone even if he was not the one who performed the action itself.

As for the actions where the performance of the act itself and the physical movements made by the immediate cause are not of primary importance, these are attributed to both the immediate and the ultimate causes. For example, acts such as killing, imprisoning, giving life, causing death, giving, showing kindness, and treating with respect are attributed both to the immediate cause and

the ultimate cause equally. In fact, it could be argued that their association with the ultimate cause is more powerful than their association with the immediate one, as if the higher cause is also higher in existence, authority, and power.

These are the fruits of philosophical discussions on this topic, which correspond to human intuitions. The Qur’an also confirms this in the clearest possible way, when God says in the aforementioned verse: Make war on

them so that Allah may punish them by your hands and humiliate them, and help you against them, and heal the hearts of a faithful folk, and remove rage from their hearts (9:14–15). This attributes the punishment inflicted upon the idolaters by the hands of the faithful to God Himself, because it makes those hands God’s implements (by your hands).

This is akin to the verse: Allah has created you and whatever you do (37:96), as the meaning of whatever you do either refers to the idols which they would make from stone, wood, or metal, in which case this refers to the material that the human beings have worked into idols and it attributes these works to the Creator in the same way as it does to the humans that made them; or this verse refers to the actions of human beings themselves, in which case the meaning is clear.

Another similar verse is: And who created all the kinds and made for you the ships and the cattle such as you ride (43:12), as it attributes the manufacture of ships to God, while it is evident that ships are something manufactured by men.

Note that all of this applies to actions being performed by conscious and free-willed agents. When it comes to those actions that do not depend upon either consciousness and free-will, such as involuntary actions, there are countless verses in the Qur’an (so many that we need not enumerate them, in fact)

that attribute them to God Himself. For example, He is the one who revives the earth, brings forth vegetation, splits the seed, sends down rain from the skies, causes rivers to flow, sets ships in motion across the sea by His command, and so on.

There is no contradiction in any of these examples between attributing these phenomena to God and simultaneously attributing them to other

natural agents and causes. This is because these different causes are arranged vertically and in sequence rather than horizontally and in parallel, so it is not as though God and other causes are acting on these phenomena independently of one another. Instead, God is acting upon these phenomena through these intermediate causes, and therefore there is no problem with identifying multiple causes for them.

As we have seen in our previous discussions, materialists find it difficult to understand how theists can attribute phenomena such as floods, earthquakes, and disease epidemics to God while today we know that there are natural causes for all of these. This stems from their confusion of a vertical hierarchy of causes with a horizontal array of them. They imagine that attributing such phenomena to natural causes refutes the contents of the Qur’an and the beliefs of the theists, who attribute such phenomena to the First Cause, to whom all matters ultimately return.

At the same time, the Ashʿarī and Muʿtazilī theologians have a strange debate about the meaning of the previous verse, Make war on them so that Allah may punish them by your hands (9:14), and other verses like it. Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī has discussed this at length in his Tafsīr, and we will summarize it below.

According to al-Rāzī, the Ashʿarīs claim that the verse, M ake war on them so that Allah may punish them by your hands, shows that human actions are created by God and that, therefore, human beings do not have free-will but are predetermined in their deeds. This is because the verse makes clear that God is the one who will punish the idolaters through killing some of them and wounding others with the hands of the faithful. This shows that the hands of the faithful are no different to the swords and spears that they wield; they are mere instruments with no say in the matter. It is God who acts and the acquisition of these acts (kasb), which is the criterion for moral responsibility (taklīf) is, therefore, an empty term.

W hat is more, this verse provides a stronger basis for the predestinarian thesis than the verse and you did not throw when you threw, rather it was Allah who threw (8:17), as this verse attributes the act of throwing to the Prophet, even if it does then negate it from him by attributing agency to God instead. On the other hand, the verse, Make war on them so that Allah may punish them by your hands, affirms that it is God who punishes them and makes the hands of the faithful instruments of this divine action without any say in it. The Muʿtazilī theologian al-Jubāʾī responds by arguing that if God punishing the disbelievers with the hands of the faithful meant this, it could also be

said that He punishes the faithful with the hands of the disbelievers, or that He rejected the prophets with their tongues, and that he cursed the faithful and reviled them with their mouths, because God created all of that. However, we cannot say this. Therefore, we know that God does not create the actions of human beings in this manner, rather they create their own actions. Based on this, when the verse attributes the punishment of the idolaters to God, this is meant in a broader sense. After all, this only transpires as a result of His

command and His grace. This is in the same vein that He attributes all acts of obedience and virtuous deeds to Himself because they take place through His commands and His assistance.

Al-Rāzī responds to al-Jubāʾī’s point by saying that the Ashʿarīs agree with al-Jubāʾī’s conclusion that their argument entails assigning bad deeds to God as well and they agree with this doctrine in principle, even if they do not necessarily express it as al-Jubāʾī has out of respect for God.

The discussions we have presented about these ideas above should be suf cient for the reader to discern the truth of the matter in this context, while also

making clear the errors that both of these theological schools have fallen into. As regards the Ashʿarī position, they are compelled to adopt it because they deny the existence of any causal relation between created things and say that God is the sole and immediate cause for all things in existence. Therefore, there is no cause in existence, whether independent of God or dependent upon Him, save God. According to them, the causal relationship that human beings observe between different created things is merely the appearance of causality. In reality, even this appearance of causality only exists because God wills it so: It is a habit that God follows in His creation, but it is not something He is bound to observe. Therefore, what we call causes and effects are all caused by God (and this is genuine causation). As for the causation that we observe between created causes and effects, there is no genuine causation here, merely the co-occurrence of two phenomena in all or the majority of cases.

However, this position entails the denial of the very idea of causality, even the causality that they have affirmed for God. After all, if all the things in existence share the same relation to one another, without any distinction between causes and effects, then there is no basis on which the human being can posit the notion of causality. Therefore, if he cannot conceive of causality, he cannot attribute it to God in the first place.

On the contrary, though, the human being expects phenomena to cause other phenomena, and is certain that the same actions will produce the same results time and again. He bases his entire life on the principle that effects follow from causes, irrespective of whether or not he believes in a Creator. This is not possible unless the human being innately believes in the principle of causality, and if it was possible for human nature to accept a denial of this principle and assert in its place the idea that all phenomena happen by pure coincidence, then his entire life would unravel because his mental or physical efforts would be rendered meaningless. Moreover, there would be no way for him to deduce the existence of a First Cause from the chains of causality that he observes amongst material phenomena.

The Qur’an itself bases its explanations on the assumption that causation is real. It assigns every good deed to God and negates the ascription of any evil deeds or sins to Him. It names Him with every beautiful name and describes Him with every good attribute. It negates from Him all mockery, absurdity, idleness, and frivolity. None of this is possible unless causality is real, and we have already explained previously how to reconcile God’s absolute power with human free-will.

Some materialists, and especially the proponents of dialectical materialism, draw the same conclusion as the Ashʿarī theologians by affirming determinism and negating human free-will. The only difference between the materialists and the Ashʿarīs is that the latter base their position on the principle of

divine occasionalism, namely that God alone is the cause of all things and that, therefore, there is no causation or free-will for the human being. By contrast, the materialists argue that human actions are merely the result of the sum of phenomena leading up to the action, and there is no human volition or freewill involved in this process. Therefore, all human actions are predetermined

and prefigured by material laws.

However, what escapes them is the fact that the relationship of a human action to the sum of phenomena that necessitated it is that of an effect to a sufficient cause (ʿilla tāmma, or ‘complete cause’), such that it does not depend on its existence for anything beyond them. Therefore, when all of these phenomena exist, the effect necessarily comes into being as well. As for the individual components of this complete cause— each of which is a necessary cause

(ʿilla nāqiṣ, ‘incomplete cause’) but not a sufficient one— their relationship to the effect is one of contingency rather than necessity, as its existence depends on the presence of other factors beyond them. Therefore, the effect will not come into being if only some of the components of its cause are present. For their existence, human actions depend upon the person, their volition, and innumerable other conditions, such as time, place, and materials.

Therefore, the relationship between the action and all of these conditions, assuming that they obtain, is one of necessity. However, the relationship of the action to the human being alone, or the human being combined with their volition to perform the actions, is a relationship of an effect to a necessary cause, which is one of contingency but not necessity. This is because the

voluntary actions of a human being emanate from his or her free-will. In other words, it is possible for them to perform the action or to abstain from it. If they perform it, then they do so based on their own volition, and if they do not perform it, this is also based on their own volition. However, whenever the action takes place, it does so necessarily because all of the conditions necessary for its existence in objective reality have been met, including human free-will. Therefore, the materialists confuse two different kinds of modal relation: The necessary (wujūb) relation that exists between an action and all of

the components of its sufficient cause taken as a whole, and the contingent (imkān) relation that exists between an action and each individual component of its sufficient cause taken separately. The latter includes human free-will. As for the Muʿtazila, their argument is that if God can be assigned the actions of the faithful, such as punishing the idolaters, this not only reduces them to mere passive instruments. W hat is more, it means that when the faithless persecute the faithful, or deny the prophets, or curse the believers, this

can also be attributed to God. They say this is definitively false and, therefore, conclude that the actions of human beings are created by themselves rather than by God.

However, while their premise is correct, the conclusion they draw from it is false, as this argument does not entail that human beings create their own actions and that these actions have no relationship with God whatsoever. This is because, as we have discussed, such actions can be assigned to God by virtue of the same relationship by which they are assigned to the people that perform them. This is because while they are the cause of the actions, God is the cause of their existence. Therefore, they are the immediate cause from whom the actions emanate, but God is the ultimate cause who brought them into being. These two relations are, in fact, a single relation with multiple facets: Immediate and ultimate, direct and indirect. This does not imply any over determination, meaning that two causes have independently produced the same effect where either one would have sufficed on its own, because these two causes are related vertically and hierarchically rather than horizontally and in parallel.

Now, if someone was to argue: ‘But this doesn’t solve the problem of both good deeds and bad deeds, and faith and infidelity all being assigned to God!’ We would respond by saying that our thesis only attributes the fact of their existence to God, but the direct action that produced these deeds in the form of movement in a particular time and place— for example, in the case of marriage or adultery, or eating permissible food or forbidden food—came from the human being, because he is the material entity that served as the locus of these movements. The one who created this being with the ability to move and act (while not being in motion Himself) is God, and this moving being came into existence because all the necessary causes and conditions of his existence were met. Therefore, God is not attributed with the actions of this being, such as marriage, adultery, or any other action he undertakes, in the same way as He is not described as ‘moving’ just because He has created something with the power of movement.

Of course, there are general categories of action that require neither movement or matter, in which case there is no problem with attributing them to

both man and God. For example, guidance and misguidance (so long as the latter does not imply that God misguided someone in the first instance) or punishment and putting to trial. Therefore, when a believer kills an idolater, this is a divine punishment for the idolater. On the other hand, when an idolater kills a believer, this is a divine trial for the believer. Furthermore, the

latter is a good thing, as it gives the believer the opportunity to earn God’s reward. And so on, and so forth.

As for what I claimed previously, namely that in adopting this as their counter-argument the M uʿtazila encountered the same problem as the Ashʿarīs, namely that they would be unable to deduce God’s existence, the explanation of this is as follows: If there existed in the world some phenomenon that was brought into being by a sole cause with no cause of its own to act upon it, this would mean that there could be phenomena in existence that depend only upon their causes, and that these causes do not depend on anything else beyond themselves for their existence. Now, it is possible for a cause to disappear and the effect to remain. Therefore, it would be possible to assign every

phenomenon in the cosmos to a cause other than the Necessary Being. In fact, one could assign the existence of the entirety of the cosmos to a cosmos that came before it and brought it into being. This previous cosmos has since ceased to exist. This would mean that everything in the cosmos produces everything else without entailing an infinite regress of causes, because at no point is there a never-ending chain of causes in existence. Therefore, it would be impossible to deduce God’s existence from such a conception of causality.

There are many other problems evident with the M uʿtazila’s thesis, which have been highlighted elsewhere. We have already discussed the relationship of the cosmos to God in the sixth part of this work, and some of what we said there is beneficial to our present discussion.

How can any monotheistic Muslim affirm that there is a creator alongside God in the literal sense of the word ‘creator,’ when God has explicitly stated: That is Allah, your Lord, the creator of all things, there is no Allah except Him

(40:62). This is a principle that has been repeatedly mentioned in the Qur’an. However, it is possible to attribute responsibility for human actions to human beings without cutting them of  from God causally. On the contrary, these verses illustrate that human actions are ultimately caused by God, even while reason tells us that the moral responsibility for these actions lies with human beings.

In conclusion, human actions are related both to their immediate causes (the human beings that perform them) and to their ultimate cause (God) in a way that does not infringe upon God’s divinity. God says: To these and to those—to all We extend the bounty of your Lord, and the bounty of your Lord is not confined (17:20).
